name: Getting Around
tagline: From your own street to a solo trip — know where you are, how to get there, and what to do when the plan falls apart.

skills.name: Know your way home
skills.gotItWhen: You know your full address and your parents' phone numbers by heart, you stay oriented in your own neighborhood, and from anywhere familiar — school, church, a friend's street — you could get yourself home.
looksLike: Asked for your address and a parent's number, you rattle off both without reaching for a device.
Walking back from the park, you can stop anywhere on the route and point toward home.
A ride falls through at a friend's house nearby, and you could walk home from there without directions.
waysToBuild: Drill your address and both parents' numbers until you can say them half-asleep, and re-test once a month.
Play the pointing game on walks: stop somewhere random, point toward home, then check.
Navigate the family car home from three familiar places, calling every turn from the back seat.

skills.name: Cross town on foot or bike
skills.gotItWhen: On foot or on your bike you handle real streets like a road user — you read the traffic before it reads you, follow the road rules for bikes, keep yourself visible and predictable, and pick sensible routes to the places you go.
looksLike: At a crossing you catch the driver's eyes before you commit — a green light is an invitation, not a guarantee.
You signal your turns and ride with traffic on your own, because that's just how riding works.
You choose the route with the bike lane and the safe crossing over the fast shortcut, and you can say why.
waysToBuild: Ride your three most-wanted routes — friend's house, store, park — with a parent trailing, talking through every decision.
Learn the bike rules of the road (signals, riding with traffic, lights at dusk) and teach them back on a family ride.
Do a solo round trip to an agreed spot, with a check-in text from the far end.

unlock.text: your roam radius grows — solo trips to the places we've agreed, no escort

skills.name: Read a map and follow directions
skills.gotItWhen: With a paper map or an app, you can orient yourself, plan a route, follow it turn by turn, and re-plan on the fly when a road closes or you drift off course.
looksLike: Handed the trail map at a state park, you find the you-are-here and pick the loop that fits the afternoon.
You navigate the family drive from the passenger seat, calling the turns before the app does.
The planned road turns out to be closed, and you work out the way around instead of handing the phone back.
waysToBuild: Be the family navigator for a month — every trip, every turn, paper or app.
Do one deliberately-lost drill: a parent drives you somewhere unfamiliar, and you navigate everyone home.
Plan and lead a walk using a paper map only, phone zipped away for emergencies.

skills.name: Ride public transit
skills.gotItWhen: You can ride a bus or train system for real — plan the trip, pay the fare, board the right vehicle going the right direction, make your transfer, and get off at the right stop — with your head up the whole way.
looksLike: You check the headsign before boarding, because the right route going the wrong way is still wrong.
The transfer window is tight, and you know exactly which platform you're walking to before the doors open.
In a city you've never visited, you work out the system from the map on the station wall.
waysToBuild: Ride your local routes with a parent three times, with you doing every step: fare, boarding, stops, transfer.
Do one 'you lead, we follow' trip where the parent is cargo and says nothing.
On the next family trip, plan and lead one transit journey from the hotel and back.

unlock.text: solo transit rides on routes you've done with us

skills.name: Find your way in a new place
skills.gotItWhen: Dropped into somewhere big and unfamiliar — an airport, a campus, a stadium — you can read the signage, find your gate or room or exit, and when the signs run out, you ask staff instead of wandering.
looksLike: First time in a new building, you find the room from its number: floor, wing, corridor.
At the airport you get from the curb to the gate — check-in, security, the tram to the right concourse — reading signs the whole way.
The signs stop making sense at the arena, and your next move is a staff member, not a guess.
waysToBuild: On the next family flight, lead the whole way through the airport — everyone follows you and the signs.
At any big venue, be the one who finds the seats, the bathrooms, and two exits.
Practice the ask: at the next confusing building, you're the one who walks up to the desk.

skills.name: Handle being lost
skills.gotItWhen: When the route dissolves and you genuinely don't know where you are, you run the drill: stop moving, get oriented, backtrack to the last ground you're sure of, pick the right stranger to ask — staff, a family, someone at a fixed post — and call in so your people know where you stand.
looksLike: You come out of a store by the wrong door, feel the world spin, and stand still until the map in your head rights itself.
On a trail the blazes disappear, and you backtrack to the last one you're certain of instead of pushing hopefully on.
Genuinely turned around downtown, you step into a shop, ask the person at the register, and text a parent your location before you move.
waysToBuild: Learn the drill as words first — stop, orient, backtrack, ask, call — and recite it until it's boring.
Run practice-lost drills: a parent walks you into an unfamiliar spot and shadows silently while you work your way out.
Learn to share your live location and drop a pin, and do it once for real from somewhere random.

skills.name: Keep a bike rolling
skills.gotItWhen: Your bike stays rideable because of you — you can fix a flat, get a dropped chain back on, check that the brakes actually bite, and set the seat where your legs want it.
looksLike: The chain drops mid-ride: greasy fingers, half a minute, rolling again.
You patch or swap a tube in the driveway with your own hands, and it holds air.
A friend's brakes feel mushy, and you're the one who tightens them up.
waysToBuild: Do one full flat-fix start to finish with a parent or a video coaching you — then do the next one alone.
Give your bike the ABC check (air, brakes, chain) once a month.
Watch a bike-shop tune-up once and ask the mechanic what wears out first.

skills.name: Plan a full route
skills.gotItWhen: For a real trip with several legs — walk, bus, walk, maybe a train — you can build the plan yourself: connections that line up, buffer built in on purpose, and a backup ready for the leg most likely to fail.
looksLike: You plan your own way across town to a class: which bus, which stop, and how much walking margin.
Your plan names its plan B: if the 4:10 bus doesn't show, here's exactly what happens instead.
You brief the family on the route to the game — legs, times, and a meeting point if anyone gets separated — and it works.
waysToBuild: Plan one real multi-leg trip a month and lead it — appointments, practices, and events all count.
Do the buffer math out loud: what's the latest bus that technically works, and which earlier one do you actually take?
For your next plan, write the plan B before you leave: which leg is most likely to fail, and what you'll do.

skills.name: Drive safely
skills.gotItWhen: Behind the wheel you drive like the stakes are real — smooth car control, speed that fits the conditions, honest following distance, phone away and out of reach — and when the road rattles you, a near-miss or a horn or a missed exit, you settle yourself and keep driving well, because you know distraction, speed, and panic kill more teen drivers than anything else.
looksLike: Your phone rides in the glovebox or a zipped bag, every trip — including the five-minute ones.
Rain starts, and your speed and following distance change before anyone suggests it.
Someone cuts you off hard with friends in the car — your hands stay quiet, your speed stays steady, and the moment stays in the rearview.
waysToBuild: Log practice hours across conditions on purpose — night, rain, highway, gravel — not just sunny errands.
Adopt the phone rule from drive one: glovebox or bag, every single trip, no exceptions to negotiate later.
Narrate one full drive out loud to your teaching parent — hazards, mirrors, gaps — so they can hear what you're seeing.

unlock.text: solo driving, expanding with your graduated license

skills.name: Keep a car alive
skills.gotItWhen: The car you drive stays healthy because of you — you keep it fueled, keep the tires at pressure and check their tread, check the oil, keep the wipers and washer fluid working, can jump-start a dead battery, and when a warning light comes on you know what it means and what to do next.
looksLike: The low-tire light comes on, and you're at the air pump that same day, gauge in hand.
You check the oil in the driveway — pull, wipe, dip, read — and know what a good level looks like.
A friend's car won't start, and you're the one hooking up the jumper cables in the right order.
waysToBuild: Do a monthly ten-minute check on the family car — tires, oil, washer fluid, lights — with a written checklist until you don't need it.
Learn the tread test and the pressure sticker inside the driver's door, then teach both to a sibling.
Jump-start a car once with a parent supervising, saying the cable order out loud as you go.
Go through the owner's manual warning-light pages once, sorting them into 'pull over now' versus 'book the shop.'

skills.name: Handle car trouble and traffic stops
skills.gotItWhen: When driving goes wrong, you know the drill and run it calmly: a flat gets you fully off the road with hazards on before anything else; a dead battery gets a safe jump or a call; a fender-bender gets photos and insurance details exchanged with no roadside argument; and at a traffic stop you pull over promptly, keep your hands visible on the wheel, and say what you're reaching for before you reach.
looksLike: A tire lets go on the highway, and you get all the way onto the shoulder, hazards on, out the passenger side — before you think about the tire.
After a parking-lot bump, you photograph everything and swap insurance info, polite and brief, leaving fault to the insurers.
Pulled over, your hands stay on the wheel and you say 'my license is in my backpack — okay if I reach for it?' before moving.
waysToBuild: Change a tire in the driveway until the whole job takes you under twenty minutes.
Run the traffic-stop script with a parent playing officer: hands, words, documents — in that order.
Build the car's trouble kit together — cables, flashlight, phone charger, insurance card — and know where everything lives.

skills.name: Book your own travel
skills.gotItWhen: You can book real travel yourself — find the right tickets at sane prices, check the times and seats before paying, know what documents the trip requires, and keep the confirmations where you can produce them at a counter.
looksLike: You book your own bus ticket to a cousin's, checking the arrival time against the pickup plan before you pay.
At check-in, the confirmation is on your screen before the agent finishes asking for it.
Booking for a family trip, you catch that the cheap flight lands at midnight — and weigh whether cheap is worth it.
waysToBuild: Book one leg of the next family trip yourself, start to finish, with the card handed over only at checkout.
Price the same trip three ways — the carrier's own site, an aggregator, in person — and find where the fees hide.
Make a confirmations folder (an email label or a screenshots album) and use it for every booking from now on.

skills.name: Take a trip on your own
skills.gotItWhen: You can plan and pull off a real trip with an overnight, no adult along — transport booked, a place to sleep arranged, a budget that survives contact with reality, check-ins that actually happen — and when something goes sideways en route, you handle it and keep the trip alive.
looksLike: You take the bus to a cousin's city for a weekend: tickets yours, transfer yours, pickup coordinated by you.
A delay eats your connection mid-trip, and the folks at home hear how you solved it after it's already solved.
You come home from a trip you planned with money left over, stories to tell, and hosts who'd have you back.
waysToBuild: Do a dry run first: a full solo day-trip to another town — there, lunch, back — with a check-in at every leg.
Plan the real trip on paper: every leg, every cost, one backup per leg — then walk a parent through it like a briefing.
Pack from your own written list, live out of the bag the whole trip, and add whatever you forgot to next trip's list.

unlock.text: 🎉 travel privileges — trips with friends or solo, planned by you, on your signature
